AI & data centers · 2026-06-21

AI Power Has Entered a Second Queue

The standard explanation for the AI power problem is that data centers are arriving faster than utilities can expand the grid. That remains true. It no longer describes the entire constraint.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-06-21 · 15 min read

In brief

  • 56 GW | GE Vernova slot reservations at the end of Q1 2026.
  • 5+ years | reported lead time for large-frame gas turbines.
  • 2.67 GW | Project Kilby’s revised capacity, with first power targeted for 2028.
  • 2028–2030 | dated turbine access is most likely to constrain turbine-led projects.
  • 36 months | the delivery threshold that would signal meaningful queue normalization.

Bypassing the grid creates a second queue

Chart

Reuters chart, “Forecast US gas turbine supply, gas plant additions”

Source shown by Reuters: Wood Mackenzie.

Open source visual from Reuters chart, “Forecast US gas turbine supply, gas plant additions”

Reuse: Reuters / Wood Mackenzie rights not verified · Attribution: Source shown by Reuters: Wood Mackenzie.

Developers are responding to interconnection delays with behind-the-meter generation, private grids, brownfield power sites and dedicated generation contracts. Once they choose that route, they enter a second queue. The project now depends on synchronizing a specific turbine or engine package, electrical equipment, fuel infrastructure, construction labor and a commercial-operation year.

The critical object is therefore not an abstract megawatt. It is a dated delivery package.

The demand backdrop explains why buyers are willing to secure equipment early. Berkeley Lab’s 2024 study estimated that U.S. data-center electricity consumption rose from 58 TWh in 2014 to about 176 TWh in 2023, with a projected range of 325–580 TWh in 2028. A subsequent Berkeley Lab update shifted the forecast horizon to 2030 and estimated that data centers could account for 9.5%–15.3% of U.S. electricity consumption, with an 11.8% midpoint. (Berkeley Lab updated outlook)

The IEA’s base case puts global data-center electricity demand on a path from about 415 TWh in 2024 to roughly 945 TWh in 2030. These scenarios do not determine the fuel mix. They explain why schedule certainty has acquired economic value. (IEA Energy and AI)

The sharper thesis is sequential. Large-frame turbine availability is not the sole AI-power bottleneck. It becomes a material gate after a developer has tried to route around the more visible grid and utility-planning constraints.

Turbine procurement is becoming a queue market

GE Vernova’s first-quarter 2026 disclosures show how this market works. The company ended the quarter with 44 GW of firm Gas Power equipment backlog and 56 GW of slot reservations, for a combined 100 GW.

During the quarter, GE added 21 GW of gas-equipment contracts. Nineteen gigawatts of that total consisted of new slot reservations; another 6 GW of previous reservations converted into firm orders, while 4 GW of equipment shipped. The 100 GW headline is therefore neither 100 GW of firm orders nor 100 GW of completed projects. It is a mixture of contracted backlog and customers holding positions in the production calendar. (GE Vernova Q1 2026 results)

Siemens Energy has also begun reporting reservation flows as a central commercial metric. It disclosed 12 GW of reservation conversions and 12 GW of new reservations in its fiscal first quarter, alongside orders for 102 gas turbines. Reservation-based procurement is now a repeatable process across major OEMs rather than an isolated GE mechanism. (Siemens Energy Q1 FY2026)

A reservation has option-like value because it preserves access to a delivery year while the developer advances offtake, financing, permits and plant design. It should not be confused with a freely tradable financial asset. Public disclosures do not establish that these positions can be assigned, refunded cheaply or sold in a transparent secondary market.

The physical scarcity is nevertheless visible. Reuters cited estimates that large-frame turbine lead times had moved beyond five years. It also reported a Wood Mackenzie estimate that the U.S. turbine-order pipeline rose from 7 GW in 2020 to 44 GW in 2025. Combined-cycle construction costs were reported at roughly $2,000–$2,500 per kilowatt, including an RMI estimate of at least $2,400 per kilowatt. Those are attributed estimates rather than a uniform industry price series. (Reuters on turbine supply)

Wood Mackenzie separately forecasts that turbine prices could reach about $600 per kilowatt by the end of 2027, 195% above 2019 levels. The important signal is not the precise price forecast. It is that manufacturing calendars, customer advances and reservation conversions have become central to project development. (Wood Mackenzie turbine outlook)

The project pipeline is a map of claimed delivery years

The named projects show what a turbine allocation can anchor—and what it cannot guarantee.

Figures are drawn from company project disclosures, OEM releases and Reuters reporting. Project dates are sponsor targets unless an operating milestone is explicitly stated.

NRG provides the clearest example of schedule packaging. Its agreement coordinates development, GE Vernova equipment and Kiewit-TIC engineering and construction. The 5.4 GW total stretches through 2032; only the first two approximately 1.2 GW phases are targeted for 2029 and 2030. The program shows how turbine capacity, EPC responsibility and standardized generating blocks can be procured together. (NRG development program)

Project Kilby shows the limits of equipment-led analysis. The Chevron-led concept originally contemplated up to 4 GW and power around 2027. The current project is approximately 2.67 GW, targets first power in 2028 and still requires a formal investment decision. Microsoft has signed a 20-year power agreement and says it will fund the generation and supporting infrastructure for its approximately 2 GW Pecos data-center campus. Customer commitment has reduced demand risk, but it has not eliminated financing, permitting, design or construction risk. (Chevron–Microsoft agreement)

Homer City and Cheyenne illustrate the value of brownfield infrastructure and named equipment allocations. Homer City plans up to 4.4 GW around seven GE 7HA.02 turbines. Tallgrass and Mitsubishi Power allocated two M501JAC units for approximately 1,150 MW at the Cheyenne Power Hub. These announcements improve schedule credibility. Neither allocation proves that the project will reach commercial operation on the stated date. (Homer City project overview) (Cheyenne turbine allocation)

Modular generation sells time in smaller increments

A developer that cannot align a large combined-cycle block with the compute schedule has alternatives. Reciprocating engines, generator sets, batteries and private-grid architectures can energize capacity in smaller increments.

Wärtsilä has announced more than 2.4 GW of U.S. data-center orders across four projects: 282 MW, 507 MW, 412 MW and 790 MW. The 790 MW Texas project will use 42 engines as its primary off-grid source, with equipment deliveries planned for 2028 and full operation expected in late 2029. The architecture offers modularity and redundancy, although it does not provide immediate relief. (Wärtsilä Texas order)

Cummins’ agreement with Circe Energy extends from 2026 through 2030 and combines natural-gas generator sets with microgrid controls, validation, operational-data sharing and service support. Circe and its engineer of record remain responsible for final system design and implementation. The package demonstrates that equipment, controls and commissioning workflow are increasingly sold together. (Cummins–Circe agreement)

Pacifico Energy’s GW Ranch goes further by combining gas generation, 1.8 GW of batteries and up to 750 MWac of solar within a private-grid campus. Pacifico reports an air permit covering up to 7.65 GW of gas generation and more than 5 GW of planned campus capacity, with first power targeted for 2027. It remains a developer plan rather than operating proof. (Pacifico GW Ranch)

These projects confirm demand for modular and integrated power procurement. They do not prove that turbine scarcity caused every engine or private-grid selection. Grid delays, phased commissioning, redundancy and load flexibility also influence the architecture.

Value moves toward whoever can contract the schedule

The scarcity premium does not remain inside the turbine casing. A reserved machine exposes the next dated requirements: transformers, switchgear, substations, generators, protection systems, gas connections, controls, cranes, commissioning teams and spare parts.

GE Vernova booked $2.4 billion of data-center-related Electrification equipment orders in the first quarter of 2026. That figure is order intake, not quarterly data-center revenue or profit. Siemens Energy has reported substantial data-center grid orders while investing in transformers, switchgear, generators, turbine components and service capacity.

These disclosures point to pull-through across the electrical stack. They should not be added to turbine, EPC and developer order values as if each represented a separate demand pool. The same plant budget can appear in several suppliers’ backlogs.

Commercial control is also splitting across participants. The turbine OEM controls access to the manufacturing calendar. The EPC contractor controls construction sequencing and interface execution. The developer controls land, permits, fuel and the project company. The hyperscaler controls load commitment, funding and acceptance of the energization schedule.

The participant that can contract across several of these interfaces can capture more value than a standalone equipment vendor. NRG’s integrated structure is one attempt. Chevron’s long-duration Microsoft agreement is another. Cummins is bundling hardware, controls, validation and service.

Recurring service economics arrive later. Original-equipment orders can eventually create demand for inspections, hot-section parts, repairs, software monitoring and long-term service agreements. That revenue generally follows shipment, commissioning, operating-hour accumulation and warranty periods. It should not be analytically booked at the same time as the original equipment sale.

Public-company exposure is therefore distributed. GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries control large-frame production and parts ecosystems. Wärtsilä and Cummins are selling modular alternatives. NRG and Chevron are moving toward integrated, contracted power supply. Kiewit-TIC represents scarce EPC execution. These are exposures to different control points, not interchangeable securities conclusions.

Manufacturing relief is real, but it arrives slowly

OEMs are responding. GE Vernova is expanding Greenville and has indicated that higher heavy-duty turbine output should begin in the second half of 2026, with annual shipments moving toward roughly 20 GW from 2027. Siemens Energy has announced a $1 billion U.S. program spanning turbines, blades and vanes, transformers, switchgear and service capacity. Mitsubishi has described plans for approximately 30% more turbine-production capacity and additional precision-casting investment. Wärtsilä is expanding technical production capacity in Vaasa by 35%.

These investments weaken any claim of permanent scarcity. They do not yet show that quoted delivery windows have normalized.

The most defensible horizon is that dated large-frame availability remains a material sequential gate for turbine-led projects seeking operation from 2028 through at least 2030. Projects entering procurement late may remain exposed beyond that period.

The tipping condition requires more than one factory announcement. Delivery windows would need to compress below roughly three years across multiple OEMs while shipments rise and reservation pools stop expanding. A declining queue caused by project cancellations would signal weakening demand, not successful industrial execution.

The historical base rate ends in overbuilding

The closest U.S. precedent is the combined-cycle construction boom of 2000–2004. Developers built large volumes of gas capacity in response to market expectations and improving turbine economics. The buildout eventually produced excess capacity.

EIA reported that combined-cycle plants designed to operate at utilization rates of 50%–70% averaged only about 34% in 2003. Construction had outrun realized demand and market conditions changed. (EIA combined-cycle history)

The similarity is coordinated overreaction. Equipment suppliers, developers and financiers can all respond to the same demand forecast, turning scarcity into surplus.

The difference is that several current projects have named hyperscaler customers, direct infrastructure funding and long-duration power agreements. Those structures can improve demand visibility. They cannot ensure that every announced campus reaches its original capacity, schedule or utilization.

Project Kilby’s revision from an up-to-4-GW concept targeting 2027 to approximately 2.67 GW targeting 2028 is already a warning against treating early announcements as fixed demand. Reservations can protect a schedule while the underlying project continues to change.

The thesis fails if another gate repeatedly determines the date

The strongest counterargument is that turbine access is visible because it is easy to count, while the actual project bottleneck may be financing, permitting, fuel infrastructure, electrical equipment or EPC execution.

Kilby has a named customer, a long-duration agreement and identified generation equipment, yet still awaits FID. That is direct evidence that securing demand and machinery is necessary but insufficient.

Regulatory relief could also reduce the importance of private generation. FERC has directed six regional grid operators to address large-load studies, co-location, behind-the-meter generation, flexible-load services, cost allocation and electrically proximate generation. Faster grid processes would give developers another route around the turbine queue. (FERC large-load action)

Reservation quality is another unresolved variable. GE’s 56 GW pool is commercially meaningful, but the public record does not disclose deposits, cancellation rights, assignment terms or delay remedies. If reservations are cheap to release, the queue may exaggerate executable demand.

No clean operating counterexample yet shows that a multi-hundred-megawatt AI campus was energized on schedule while large-frame availability proved irrelevant. The engine and private-grid cases remain mostly in procurement, construction or planned deployment.

The evidence therefore supports a narrower conclusion: dated turbine access is a current sequential constraint for turbine-led projects, not the dominant AI-power gate or a sufficient predictor of completion.

What to watch

  • By December 31, 2026, Project Kilby reaches formal FID with financing, permits and notice to proceed.
  • By June 30, 2027, two major OEMs offer standard large-frame delivery within 36 months.
  • GE’s backlog-plus-reservations decline for two consecutive quarters while shipments rise without cancellation-driven attrition.
  • By December 31, 2027, Circe supplies at least 100 MW to data-center load for 30 consecutive days.
  • By December 31, 2030, at least 1 GW of the named large-frame cohort reaches verified operation.
